--- title: "VAR analysis" subtitle: "Industrial production and University of Michigan consumer sentiment" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/setup.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tseries) # adf.test library(urca) # ur.kpss, ca.jo library(vars) # VARselect, VAR, causality, irf, fevd }) umc_ts <- read_monthly_ts("data/umcsent.csv") fmt_p <- function(p) { if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16") if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE))) paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p)) } # Johansen test statistics next to their critical values johansen_table <- function(jo) { data.frame( Hypothesis = rownames(jo@cval), Statistic = round(jo@teststat, 2), jo@cval, check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) } ``` ::: The second series is the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment (UMCSENT), a monthly survey of how US households see current and future economic conditions. The question is whether consumer sentiment carries information about future industrial production. ## Consumer sentiment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(umc_ts) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (1966:Q1 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![University of Michigan consumer sentiment (1966:Q1 = 100)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-umcsent-1.png){#fig-umcsent width=768} ::: ::: Unlike industrial production, sentiment has no clear upward trend but large cyclical swings. It falls in the 2001 recession, the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic; its lowest value in the sample is 50 (Jun 2022). ## Stationarity of UMCSENT ::: {#tbl-umc-tests .cell tbl-cap='KPSS statistics and ADF p-values, UMCSENT in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} umc_kpss <- sapply(c(tau = "tau", mu = "mu"), function(type) ur.kpss(umc_ts, type = type)@teststat) adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24) umc_adf <- data.frame( Lag = adf_lags, `ADF p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(umc_ts, k = k)$p.value)), check.names = FALSE ) umc_pp <- PP.test(umc_ts) umc_adf ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| ADF p-value| |---:|-----------:| | 1| 0.0815742| | 2| 0.2458332| | 3| 0.2872010| | 4| 0.3761136| | 5| 0.5352488| | 12| 0.3621571| | 24| 0.3984279|
::: ::: 1. The KPSS statistics (0.3588 with trend and 1.3267 with a constant) are above the 5% critical values (0.146 and 0.463), so stationarity in levels is rejected. 2. All ADF p-values are above 0.05 and the Phillips-Perron test gives p = 0.2266, so the unit root cannot be rejected. All three tests agree: UMCSENT is not stationary in levels. ## Cointegration (Johansen test) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dset <- cbind(ip_ts, umc_ts) colnames(dset) <- c("IPB", "UMCSENT") lag_select <- VARselect(dset, lag.max = 8, type = "const") lag_select$selection ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AIC(n) HQ(n) SC(n) FPE(n) 8 3 2 8 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} johansen_trace <- ca.jo(dset, type = "trace", ecdet = "const", K = 4) johansen_eigen <- ca.jo(dset, type = "eigen", ecdet = "const", K = 4) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-johansen .cell tbl-cap='Johansen test: trace (top) and maximum eigenvalue (bottom)'} ```{.r .cell-code} jo_trace <- johansen_table(johansen_trace) jo_eigen <- johansen_table(johansen_eigen) jo_trace ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Hypothesis | Statistic| 10pct| 5pct| 1pct| |:-------------|---------:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |r <= 1 | | 4.83| 7.52| 9.24| 12.97| |r = 0 | | 14.95| 17.85| 19.96| 24.60|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} jo_eigen ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Hypothesis | Statistic| 10pct| 5pct| 1pct| |:-------------|---------:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |r <= 1 | | 4.83| 7.52| 9.24| 12.97| |r = 0 | | 10.12| 13.75| 15.67| 20.20|
::: ::: For r = 0, both the trace statistic (14.95) and the maximum eigenvalue statistic (10.12) are below their 5% critical values (19.96 and 15.67). The null hypothesis r = 0 cannot be rejected: there is no cointegrating relationship, so no stable long-run link between industrial production and consumer sentiment. A VECM is therefore not estimated; instead, a VAR is fitted to the first differences of both series to make them stationary. ## First differences ::: {#tbl-diff-tests .cell tbl-cap='ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values for the differenced series'} ```{.r .cell-code} dset_diff <- data.frame( IPB_d = diff(as.numeric(ip_ts)), UMCSENT_d = diff(as.numeric(umc_ts)) ) diff_tests <- data.frame( Series = names(dset_diff), `ADF p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x)$p.value)), `PP p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) PP.test(x)$p.value), check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) diff_tests ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Series | ADF p-value| PP p-value| |:---------|-----------:|----------:| |IPB_d | 0.01| 0.01| |UMCSENT_d | 0.01| 0.01|
::: ::: For both differenced series the ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values are 0.01 (below 0.05), so the unit root is rejected: both series are stationary after differencing and can be used in the VAR. ## VAR lag selection and estimation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_lag <- VARselect(dset_diff, lag.max = 12, type = "const") var_lag$selection ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AIC(n) HQ(n) SC(n) FPE(n) 12 12 12 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} var_model <- VAR(dset_diff, p = 4, type = "const") ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-var-ipb .cell tbl-cap='VAR(4), equation for the change in industrial production (IPB_d)'} ```{.r .cell-code} var_summary <- summary(var_model) ipb_eq <- var_summary$varresult$IPB_d$coefficients umc_eq <- var_summary$varresult$UMCSENT_d$coefficients round(ipb_eq, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) IPB_d.l1 -0.3456 0.0488 -7.0753 0.0000 UMCSENT_d.l1 0.0427 0.0206 2.0704 0.0390 IPB_d.l2 -0.1271 0.0517 -2.4585 0.0144 UMCSENT_d.l2 0.0210 0.0208 1.0112 0.3125 IPB_d.l3 -0.0261 0.0517 -0.5052 0.6137 UMCSENT_d.l3 0.0088 0.0208 0.4245 0.6714 IPB_d.l4 -0.1501 0.0488 -3.0779 0.0022 UMCSENT_d.l4 -0.0155 0.0208 -0.7443 0.4571 const 0.1543 0.0858 1.7972 0.0730 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-var-umc .cell tbl-cap='VAR(4), equation for the change in consumer sentiment (UMCSENT_d): lags of IPB_d'} ```{.r .cell-code} round(umc_eq[grep("^IPB_d", rownames(umc_eq)), ], 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) IPB_d.l1 0.0440 0.1169 0.3765 0.7068 IPB_d.l2 -0.1558 0.1238 -1.2580 0.2091 IPB_d.l3 0.0668 0.1239 0.5390 0.5902 IPB_d.l4 -0.0027 0.1168 -0.0233 0.9814 ``` ::: ::: 1. The information criteria suggest 12 lags; p = 4 is used to keep the model parsimonious and easy to interpret. 2. In the industrial production equation, sentiment one month earlier (`UMCSENT_d.l1`) has a positive coefficient (0.043) that is significant at 5% (p = 0.0390): an improvement in consumer confidence is followed by higher industrial production the next month. 3. In the sentiment equation, none of the lags of industrial production is significant. The VAR(4) suggests a one-directional short-run relationship, from consumer sentiment to industrial production. ## VAR diagnostics ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_serial <- serial.test(var_model, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic") var_arch <- vars::arch.test(var_model, lags.multi = 12, multivariate.only = TRUE) var_norm <- normality.test(var_model, multivariate.only = TRUE) data.frame( Test = c("Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags)", "Multivariate ARCH (12 lags)", "Jarque-Bera (normality)"), `p-value` = signif(c( var_serial$serial$p.value, var_arch$arch.mul$p.value, var_norm$jb.mul$JB$p.value ), 3), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Test | p-value| |:--------------------------------------|-------:| |Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags) | 0e+00| |Multivariate ARCH (12 lags) | 3e-07| |Jarque-Bera (normality) | 0e+00|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stability_model <- stability(var_model, type = "OLS-CUSUM") plot(stability_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![OLS-CUSUM stability test for each VAR equation](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-cusum-1.png){#fig-cusum width=768} ::: ::: The diagnostic tests all give p < 0.05, indicating residual autocorrelation, ARCH effects and non-normality, which reflect the macroeconomic shocks of 1990–2025. In the OLS-CUSUM plot, the empirical fluctuation process stays within the critical bands for both equations, so the parameters of the VAR(4) are stable over the sample. The model is used for the causality analysis and the forecast below. ## Granger causality ::: {#tbl-granger .cell tbl-cap='Granger causality tests (F-tests on all four lags)'} ```{.r .cell-code} granger_ipb <- causality(var_model, cause = "IPB_d") granger_umc <- causality(var_model, cause = "UMCSENT_d") data.frame( Direction = c("IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d", "UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d"), `F statistic` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$statistic, granger_umc$Granger$statistic), 4), `p-value` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value, granger_umc$Granger$p.value), 4), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Direction | F statistic| p-value| |:------------------|-----------:|-------:| |IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d | 0.8540| 0.4912| |UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d | 1.5772| 0.1784|
::: ::: 1. IPB_d → UMCSENT_d: p = 0.4912 (> 0.05); changes in industrial production do not help predict consumer sentiment. 2. UMCSENT_d → IPB_d: the joint p-value for the four lags is 0.1784 (> 0.05), so at the 5% level the null hypothesis of no Granger causality cannot be rejected. 3. The first lag of sentiment was individually significant in the VAR, but the Granger test evaluates all four lags together, and lags 2–4 are not significant, which weakens the joint F-test. The information link between the two variables appears only at a very short horizon (one month) and fades over a four-month window. ## Impulse response functions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(123) # bootstrap confidence bands irf_umc_to_ipb <- irf( var_model, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d", n.ahead = 20, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90 ) plot(irf_umc_to_ipb, main = "Shock to UMCSENT_d, response of IPB_d") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Response of IPB_d to a shock in UMCSENT_d (90% bootstrap bands)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-irf-umc-1.png){#fig-irf-umc width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} irf_ipb_to_umc <- irf( var_model, impulse = "IPB_d", response = "UMCSENT_d", n.ahead = 20, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90 ) plot(irf_ipb_to_umc, main = "Shock to IPB_d, response of UMCSENT_d") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Response of UMCSENT_d to a shock in IPB_d (90% bootstrap bands)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-irf-ipb-1.png){#fig-irf-ipb width=768} ::: ::: 1. A positive shock to consumer sentiment raises industrial production in the following month, and the effect is statistically significant (the bootstrap band is entirely above zero). The effect is temporary and dies out after about five months. 2. For a shock to industrial production, the zero line stays inside the confidence band: production shocks have no significant effect on consumer confidence. This supports the view of sentiment indicators as leading indicators of real industrial activity. ## Forecast error variance decomposition ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fevd_result <- fevd(var_model, n.ahead = 10) plot(fevd_result) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forecast error variance decomposition (10 months)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-fevd-1.png){#fig-fevd width=768} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-fevd .cell tbl-cap='Share of forecast error variance at a 10-month horizon'} ```{.r .cell-code} fevd_10 <- rbind( IPB_d = fevd_result$IPB_d[10, ], UMCSENT_d = fevd_result$UMCSENT_d[10, ] ) round(100 * fevd_10, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` IPB_d UMCSENT_d IPB_d 98.83 1.17 UMCSENT_d 0.93 99.07 ``` ::: ::: 1. In the first month, almost 100% of the variance of each variable is explained by its own shocks. 2. At a 10-month horizon, changes in consumer sentiment explain about 1.17% of the forecast error variance of industrial production. 3. In the other direction, industrial production explains only 0.93% of the variance of consumer sentiment. The decomposition supports a one-sided, short-run relationship: sentiment plays a small but stable role as a leading indicator for industry. ## VAR forecast ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_forecast <- predict(var_model, n.ahead = 24, ci = 0.90) fc_ipb_diff <- var_forecast$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"] # Rebuild index levels by adding the forecast changes to the last observed value last_ipb <- tail(as.numeric(ip_ts), 1) fc_ipb_level <- cumsum(c(last_ipb, fc_ipb_diff))[-1] history_time <- as.numeric(time(ip_ts)) last_time_point <- tail(history_time, 1) forecast_time <- seq(last_time_point + 1 / 12, by = 1 / 12, length.out = length(fc_ipb_level)) df_ipb <- data.frame( time = c(history_time, forecast_time), value = c(as.numeric(ip_ts), fc_ipb_level) ) ggplot(df_ipb, aes(x = time, y = value)) + geom_line() + geom_vline(xintercept = last_time_point, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![VAR forecast of industrial production, 24 months ahead (dashed line = end of data)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-var-forecast-1.png){#fig-var-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. `predict()` forecasts the next 24 months with a 90% interval. 2. Because the VAR is estimated on differences, the forecasts are monthly changes. 3. They are converted back to index levels with `cumsum()`, adding the forecast changes to the last observed value (99.33). 4. To the right of the dashed red line, industrial production grows steadily and moderately, to 102.12 after 24 months, supported by the positive impulse from consumer sentiment.
